newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australia's Howard warns against republic division.
newsitem.headline: Australia's Howard warns against republic division.

text.p: Australian Prime Minister John Howard said on Monday the country needed a clear majority decision on whether to become a republic, severing ties with Britain's monarchy, not a close vote that left it disunited.

"In my judgment the worst possible outcome on this issue would be to have a referendum, say in the year 2000, which was defeated by 51 percent to 49, or for that matter carried 51 percent to 49," Howard told Australian Broadcasting Corp Radio.
Opinion polls generally show half or just over half of Australians favour removing Britain's monarch as head of state.

Howard said he was still committed to ensuring the Australian people had a vote on the issue by the end of the century, a policy he took to the March election in which he ousted his republican predecessor Paul Keating.

"Nor have I altered my view that if the Australian nation is to become a republic (then) it should become a republic in circumstances which unite rather than divide the Australian community," he said.
"It's one of those things where if we are going to change it's got to be something that the overwhelming bulk of the community are taken along with," he said.
A key element of Howard's policy is a convention to discuss republic proposals before a national referendum.
Delegates to the convention were supposed to be elected, but he now says they might be appointed instead.
"There are a number of options that can produce an outcome where a lot of people participate in producing that outcome," Howard said.

"I am not a republican, but I have always said that I am going to facilitate debate, facilitate process, facilitate an expression of public opinion and the proper ultimate decision-making process, if that is what the Australian people clearly want," Howard said.
Keating launched a campaign in 1991 to sever ties with Britain by the end of the century. Howard's critics say he has let the republican push lose momentum.
